content:
Jordan Lee: Kicking off a thread on fairness for shared burst pools. We need to pick between token bucket vs WFQ (or hybrid), AND make admission deterministic even with telemetry lag (utilization + queue depth + pool headroom). I’m worried we end up with “it depends on which replica saw which telemetry at t”.

Keiko Yamamoto: +1. From infra side, determinism matters for replay/debugging. Also need to avoid over-admitting when GPU telemetry is delayed (common during spikes).

Ravi Menon: Routing angle: if admission isn’t deterministic, we’ll get weird flapping and retries amplify load. We need a consistent “decision function” per request.

Mina Haddad: For routing, we can tolerate some “deny then later allow” behavior IF denial reason codes are stable + we have clear retry hints. But if two identical requests get different decisions in the same second, customers will see chaos.

Ethan Park: Control plane/policy engine can help: we can define inputs that admission is allowed to use. Eg: only use telemetry snapshot with an explicit `snapshot_id` (monotonic), not “latest” at evaluation time.

Benji Okafor: Implementation note: we’re likely running multiple admission controller pods per region. If they each cache telemetry, they’ll drift.

Allison Grant: Observability: if we can tag every decision with `telemetry_age_ms` and `snapshot_id`, we can at least explain things. But we should still aim for deterministic per-snapshot.

Jordan Lee: Exactly. Two related decisions:
1) Fairness model: token bucket vs WFQ.
2) Determinism: how to avoid per-replica randomness under lag.

Keiko Yamamoto: Re: fairness: token bucket is simpler + can encode cooldown and max burst ratio easily. WFQ is “fairer” but depends on accurate queue measurement and schedule.

Ravi Menon: WFQ also implies a queueing system (or at least virtual finish times). Are we actually queueing burst requests? Or are we just gating and returning immediate deny/429?

Jordan Lee: Current ADR draft leans “immediate deny” for most, optional short queue window (like 200-500ms) if we can do it safely. So not a big centralized queue.

Mina Haddad: If we’re not queueing centrally, WFQ starts to feel like we’re re-implementing WFQ in a stateless service. That’s hard.

Peter Holtz: SRE view: token bucket is more predictable. WFQ tends to create “mystery math” for oncall. Also under incident conditions, it’s easier to crank down refill rates / caps.

Jordan Lee: Agree. But token bucket has a nasty property: under telemetry lag, you might keep refilling/admitting even when pool is already saturated, unless you clamp.

Keiko Yamamoto: We can clamp with a global “pool headroom” signal. But then fairness isn’t just per-tenant; it’s gated by pool state.

Allison Grant: Telemetry lag: what’s our worst-case? We’ve seen 10-30s staleness from DCGM exporters when nodes are thrashing.

Logan Wright: Yep. Especially when Prometheus scrape is behind. Also aggregation jobs can lag. Anything dependent on “real-time utilization” is risky.

Ethan Park: That suggests we should not rely on fine-grained utilization. Prefer coarse signals: allocated slots from scheduler (authoritative) rather than measured GPU util.

Benji Okafor: Do we have an authoritative “allocated GPUs in burst pool” number? Terraform + scheduler knows desired counts, but “in use” is tricky.

Keiko Yamamoto: We have two signals:
- Control plane knows configured pool size (N GPUs)
- Data plane can emit “active batcher slots” / “inflight reqs” more directly than GPU util
Those can still lag, but less than DCGM.

Ravi Menon: For determinism, could we do:
- Admission decision uses *only* (1) static config + (2) a replicated in-memory token bucket state using a single store (Redis?)
- Pool saturation uses a separate “circuit breaker” that is conservative if telemetry age > threshold

Peter Holtz: Please no Redis dependency in the hot path unless we’re 100% comfortable. But a lightweight strongly-consistent store is how you get “same answer from all replicas”.

Jordan Lee: I’m trying to avoid a hard dependency on central storage per request. But we need deterministic fairness across replicas.

Mina Haddad: What about sticky hashing requests to an admission shard? e.g., hash(tenant_id, pool_id) -> shard. Then state is local and deterministic per tenant.

Benji Okafor: That works until a shard dies and we reassign. But we can accept a “state reset” with audit events.

Ethan Park: Sticky hashing + consistent hashing ring could work. Determinism becomes “deterministic given shard mapping version”. We can record `ring_version` in decision.

Allison Grant: +1, as long as metrics include `ring_version` and we alert on high churn.

Keiko Yamamoto: Fairness wise, token bucket per tenant per pool with refill rate = reserved_baseline * max_burst_ratio? Then global cap ensures fleet safety.

Jordan Lee: Here’s a strawman hybrid:
- Per-tenant token bucket for burst credits (GPU-seconds or “slots”) with refill per second.
- Optional priority tiers affect refill multiplier.
- Global pool guard: if pool_saturation > S, deny burst regardless of token bucket.
- Under telemetry lag: if `telemetry_age_ms > X`, we switch pool guard into conservative mode (deny new burst unless tenant is under a small “safe minimum”).

Ravi Menon: If we do token bucket in terms of “GPU-seconds”, we need to estimate cost of a request at admission time. That’s hard for LLM inference (var seq len).

Mina Haddad: We can estimate via request metadata: max_tokens, model class, maybe prompt tokens if known. Not perfect but better than nothing.

Peter Holtz: SRE would prefer “admit based on concurrency slots” not exact GPU-seconds. GPU-seconds metering can happen after the fact for billing.

Keiko Yamamoto: +1. Concurrency slot is a crisp control. Billing can meter actual usage.

Jordan Lee: So fairness token bucket uses “burst slots” instead of GPU-seconds. Then determinism is easier.

Logan Wright: Slot-based tokens also reduce label/cardinality headaches in metrics. GPU-seconds by model+tenant tends to explode.

Allison Grant: Determinism detail: if we’re using a token bucket, we need a clear rule on time. If each pod uses local wall clock, drift causes inconsistencies.

Ethan Park: We can use fixed windows: e.g., 1s buckets keyed by `floor(now_ms / 1000)`. But again “now” differs per pod.

Benji Okafor: If we shard by tenant/pool, then local “now” drift only affects that shard. Still not ideal.

Jordan Lee: Could use monotonic time source from the telemetry snapshot itself. Eg snapshot has `snapshot_ts_ms`; admission uses that (not local now) for token refills.

Keiko Yamamoto: That ties fairness to telemetry freshness though. Under lag, refills stall -> that’s conservative (good). But may punish tenants if telemetry pipeline is behind for unrelated reasons.

Peter Holtz: Conservative during telemetry issues is acceptable IMO. Better to deny burst than melt neighbors.

Mina Haddad: Customer experience: if telemetry lag causes burst denial, we need a denial reason that says that explicitly, not just “capacity unavailable”.

Allison Grant: Yes. Denial reasons should include `TELEMETRY_STALE` or similar. And `telemetry_age_ms` in internal debug.

Ravi Menon: Routing can then treat `TELEMETRY_STALE` as “retry with jitter” vs `POOL_SATURATED` as “backoff longer / accept baseline”.

Jordan Lee: WFQ side: any strong arguments we’re missing? It gives better fairness under contention without tuning token refill rates.

Keiko Yamamoto: WFQ assumes you can measure demand and schedule. Here we’re doing admission control, not scheduling. We’d approximate WFQ with tokens anyway.

Peter Holtz: Also WFQ w/ priorities can starve lower tiers if misconfigured. Token bucket can implement anti-starvation with min refill floor.

Ethan Park: Policy engine can express “min guaranteed burst slots per minute” for non-gold tiers if we want. That’s basically token bucket with floors.

Benji Okafor: Determinism proposal summary:
- Consistent hash shard by (tenant_id, pool_id)
- Each shard maintains token buckets in-memory
- Refill based on `snapshot_ts_ms` from telemetry feed
- Record `snapshot_id` and `ring_version` on every decision
- If `telemetry_age_ms > X`, set guardrail `deny_new_burst=true` except allow baseline

Allison Grant: Works for me. We should add metrics:
- `burst_admission_decisions_total{reason=...}`
- `burst_telemetry_age_ms` (histogram)
- `burst_ring_version_changes_total`

Mina Haddad: From routing: please guarantee determinism at least per request-id. If customer retries same request, we should avoid double-spend of tokens.

Jordan Lee: Good call. Admission should accept an idempotency key (request_id) and keep a short-lived cache of decisions per key on the shard.

Ravi Menon: That also helps avoid “retry storm consumes extra tokens”.

Peter Holtz: Make sure the cache has bounded memory + eviction. And it should be behind the feature flag at first.

Keiko Yamamoto: Next step: I’ll add notes to ADR: choose token bucket (slot-based) + shard-based determinism + telemetry-stale conservative mode.

Jordan Lee: I’ll update the fairness ADR with this hybrid and explicitly call out why WFQ isn’t a fit without centralized queue/scheduler. Please comment if objections.

Allison Grant: :thumbsup: also add a section on “debuggability”: snapshot_id, telemetry_age, ring_version, idempotency_key.

Ethan Park: :+1: I’ll sync with Benji on how to surface snapshot_id in the policy evaluation response so we can log it consistently.

Benji Okafor: Cool. I’ll prototype the consistent hashing shard map and see what it looks like with k8s pod churn.

Peter Holtz: +1, and please add a failure mode note: on shard reassignment, we should temporarily deny burst (or reset tokens to conservative) to avoid accidental over-admit.

Jordan Lee: Noted. We’ll treat shard changes as “cooldown event” for that tenant/pool for a short period unless we can persist state.

Mina Haddad: Sounds good. If we do that, denial reason should be `SHARD_REBALANCE` (internal at least) so Support doesn’t panic.

Jordan Lee: Got it. Closing the loop here; I’ll post the updated ADR link once pushed.
